title: How To Handle Being Hated For Great Classroom Management
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses a phenomenon he says SCM readers report repeatedly: excelling at classroom management can provoke resentment and even sabotage from colleagues. He argues this hostility is not unique to teaching but occurs whenever someone pursues excellence, because their success removes others' excuses and holds up an uncomfortable mirror. The article advises against confronting or seeking revenge on resentful colleagues, framing such behavior as self-defeating and beneath the teacher who has earned genuine success. Instead, he recommends quietly holding eye contact in hallway encounters as a subtle way of signaling awareness without conflict, while otherwise ignoring the behavior and continuing to improve. The piece closes on the idea that sustained excellence eventually converts detractors into admirers, and that the deeper reward of impacting students outweighs the discomfort of being disliked along the way.
points: Excelling at classroom management can provoke resentment, gossip, and sabotage from colleagues, a pattern the author says recurs across any pursuit of excellence.
Resentment from others often stems from the discomfort of seeing what they could achieve if they put in similar effort.
The recommended response is to avoid confrontation or revenge, since it drags the teacher down to the level of the person causing trouble.
Holding a colleague's gaze calmly in hallway encounters can quietly signal awareness of their behavior without direct confrontation.
Sustained, undeniable success tends to eventually convert detractors into people who want to associate with the successful teacher.
quotes: If you’re exceptional at classroom management, your colleagues will hate you for it.
The truth is, it doesn’t matter the endeavor. If you pursue excellence in any area of your life , many people, including your closest friends, won’t like it.
These are the sorriest souls who, as Thoreau mused, “are living lives of quiet desperation,” only feeling satisfaction in seeing you stumble.

Let them fade into your background. Highlight the beauty and inspiration around you and allow them to fall away from your attention. Do not attempt to get your own revenge. It will drag you down to their level, which is what they want.

You’re merely forcing them to confront the truth. It tells them oh so subtly that you’re on to them. You don’t have to say anything, though hello is okay. Be pleasant, but hold their eyes until they look away.
Funny, when you get to a certain level of success—undeniable success—again in any endeavor, everyone wants to be your friend. Those same vampires become sycophants, hoping to steal some of your mojo.
